rules: In legal writing, the standard rule is to use footnotes.
Textual footnotes contain peripheral information that is relevant but would detract from the thrust of the argument if placed in the main text.
Citation footnotes are used to indicate the source which an argument or quotation has been drawn from.
Both textual and citation information can occur within a singular footnote.
Citation footnotes ALWAYS end with a period.
At the first reference to the source.
At every subsequent quotation from the source.
At every subsequent reference or allusion to a particular passage in the source.

topics.topic: How to Indicate Footnotes in Text
rules: Footnotes are indicated by superscripted numbers.
Generally, place the footnote at the end of the sentence, after the punctuation.
When you reference a specific word or phrase in a sentence, place a footnote beside it.
When using a quote, cite your source every time you use the thoughts, words, opinions, etc. of others.
examples: The "cow jumped over the moon"¹ is a popular phrase found in books for children.
You must cite your source "every time you use the thoughts words opinions, etc. of others."²

rules: Never place more than one footnote number at any given point in the main text.
Combine the supporting citation into one footnote.
Separate different citations in a footnote with a semicolon and end the entire footnote with a period.
examples: Historical trauma theory is a branch of research that explores the multigenerational effect of a mass trauma event.¹

Footnote 1: See, Maria Yellow Horse Brave Heart, "The Historical Trauma Response" (2003) 35:1 Journal of Psychoactive Drugs 7; Les B. Whitbeck et al, "Conceptualizing and Measuring Historical Trauma" (2004) 35:3-4 American Journal of Community Psychology 1; Teresa Evans Campbell, "Historical Trauma" (2008) 23:3 Journal of Interpersonal Violence 316.

rules: Use introductory signals to indicate the relationship between the source and the proposition.

signals.meaning: The source cited directly supports the proposition.
The source cited provides added support for the proposition but is not the most authoritative or is not directly on point.
The source cited is in partial disagreement with the proposition but does not directly contradict it.
The source cited is one of several that support that proposition, but the other supporting sources are not cited.
The source cited supports and provides background information relevant to the proposition.
The source cited is the strongest of several that support the proposition.

rules: Only create a short form if you will be using the same reference throughout your paper/work.
Use the full title the first time you cite.
Always italicize the title if it is a case or legislation.
Abbreviations of articles/monographs do not need to be italicized.
examples: 1 R v Gladue, [1999] 1 SCR 688. [Gladue]
2 Maria Yellow Horse Brave Heart, "Historical Trauma Response" (2003) 41:4 American Journal of Psychology 4. [Brave Heart]
3 Criminal Code of Canada, RSD 1985, c C-46. [Code].
4 Achille Mbembe, "Necropolitcs" (2003) 15:1 Public Culture 80. [Mbembe].
8 Mbembe, supra note 4 at 82
14 Gladue, supra note 1 at para 56.
20 Code, supra note 3 at s.718.2(e).

rules: Ibid means 'in the same place'.
Use 'Ibid' to direct the reader to the immediately preceding reference.
Ibid may be used after a full citation, after a supra, or even after another Ibid.
examples: 1 R v Gladue, [1999] 1 SCR 688.
2 Ibid at para 64.
3 Ibid.

rules: Supra means 'above'.
Use the short form, in combination with supra to refer to the footnote containing the original full citation.
Do not use supra to refer to another supra or ibid.
examples: 1 R v Gladue, [1999] 1 SCR 688. [Gladue]
2 Maria Yellow Horse Brave Heart, "Historical Trauma Response" (2003) 4:3 American Community of Psychology 3. [Brave Heart]
3 Gladue, supra note 1 at para 64.
12 Achille Mbembe "Necropolitics" (2003) 15:1 Public Culture 80. [Mbembe]
15 Gladue, supra note 1 at para 81.

rules: Short quotation of four lines or fewer: place in quotation marks and incorporate directly into the text.
Long quotation of more than four lines: indent from both margins (in MS Word, indent 1.25 cm on either side) and single space. Do not use quotation marks.
examples: Sinema explained that in the context of genocides, we often "choose not to notice" if we are directly affected as a result of the conflict.¹

rules: It is acceptable to quote in a footnote to add additional context.
examples: I primarily study historical trauma as proposed by Dr. Maria Yellow Horse Brave Heart. Historical trauma has been further studied by researchers such as Dr. Teresa Evans-Campbell¹, Dr. Les Whitbeck² and Drs. Amy Bombay, Kim Matheson & Hymie Anisman³
Footnotes:
1 Evans Campbell explained her approach as "XXX..." [citation].
2 Whitbeck explained his approach as "XXX..." [citation].
3 Bombay, Matheson & Asniman explained their approach as "XXX..." [citation].

rules: Divide bibliographies into sections: Legislation, Jurisprudence, Secondary materials.
If a source does not fit into a defined section, a residual section entitled 'other materials' may be used.
Within each section, list entries in alphabetical order.
Sort legislation by title.
Sort jurisprudence by style of cause.
Sort secondary material by author's surname.
Include any initials as written on the source, even if this leads to different versions of the author's name in subsequent references.
If there is more than one author, use the surname for only the first author: Smith, John, William Jones & Timothy Adams.
If there are more than three authors, write et al. after the first name: Smith, John et al.
Insert a hanging indent of 0.63 cm for each citation so that the second and subsequent lines are indented.
The bibliography should be single spaced.
examples: Brave Heart, Maria Yellow Horse, "The historical trauma response among natives and its relationship with substance abuse: a Lakota illustration" (2003) 35:1 Journal of Psychoactive Drugs 7.

topics.template: Author, | "title of article" | (year) | volume: | issue | abbreviation of journal | first page | pinpoint.
rules: Italicize titles of journals and books; article titles go in quotation marks.
Indicate the author's name as presented on the title page of the article. Include professional titles as required.
If there are two authors, separate the names with an ampersand (&).
If there are three authors, separate the first two with a comma and place an ampersand before the last one.
If there are more than three authors, include only the first author's name and et al.
Place the title of the article in quotation marks. Do not put a comma after the title.
Separate a title from a subtitle with a colon.
Capitalize the title and use punctuation according to the conventions of the language of the title.
Always use double quotation marks, regardless of the language.
Indicate the year of publication in parentheses. If there are multiple years, separate with a dash (e.g., 2010-2011).
Place the volume number after the year of publication, followed by a colon and the issue number. Do not put spaces before and after the colon.
If the issue number is unavailable, omit it.
Where two issues are published at once, separate the numbers with a slash (6/7).
Indicate the first page of the article after the title of the journal. Do not include 'at' before the first page.
**abbreviations of journals are fine, PROVIDED that they are universal. Do not create your own abbreviation.**
examples: John Borrows, "Creating an Indigenous Legal Community" (2005) 50:1 McGill LJ 153 at 155.
Lynn A Iding, "In a Poor State: The Long Road to Human Rights Protection on the Basis of Social Condition" (2003) 41:2 Alta LR 513.

Rafael La Porta et al, "Law and Finance" (1998) 106:6 Journal of Political Economy 1113 at 1152.

RRA Walker, "The English Property Legislation of 1922-26" (1928) 10:1 J Comp Legis & Intl L (3rd) 1.
Eric David, "Pourquoi aime-t-on une musique?" (2022) RQDI (special edition, January).

rules: A citation (on one line) includes: the 'style of cause' (parties). If there are intervenors they are not listed.
Plus the neutral citation (not all older cases have them).
And a locator or source (Reporter). Not all decisions are reported.
With an indicator of the court if this is not obvious from the neutral citation or source.
Generally, you should give parallel citations (more than one way to locate the case).
Neutral citation first (if available).
Reported citation next. Rules: Official first, then semi/unofficial, then national; then general; then regional; then subject specific.
If unpublished (unreported), you may use the database file number (eg. OJ no #) and you should say which database source in brackets ... but only if unreported.
examples: Smith v Jones, 2009 SCC 23.
Smith v Jones, 2009 SCC 23, [2009] 2 SCR 98, 23 DLR (5th) 156.

rules: Pinpoints are to page or paragraph numbers.
More recent reports will have paragraph numbers; older cases may use page numbering.
Do not cite to page numbers in online sources (as they are not fixed but variable depending on how viewed).
If using page numbers, indicate which Reporter you are citing to in your footnote.
The page numbers may NOT be embedded in the online report in which case you are expected to go back to the hard copy book to obtain and cite correct page numbers.
Must include the neutral cite 1st (if available).
examples: R v King, 2002 SCC 10.
Twins v Canada (Attorney General), 2016 FC 537 (CanLII), [2017] 1 FCR 79.

rules: Means 'in the same place'.

rules: Means 'above'.

examples: 1. Hartman v Irwin, 2005 BCCA 267.

examples: *Constitution Act, 1982*, s 35, being Schedule B to the *Canada Act 1982* (UK), 1982, c 11.

rules: When citing a particular point in time, and the standard citation form is inadequate, use 'as it appeared on [day month year]' or 'as it appeared on [month year]' to clarify the point in time cited.
examples: Income Tax Act, RSC 1985, c 1 (5th Supp), s 20(1)(c) as it appeared on 12 October 2012.

rules: For statutes that appear in an appendix, always provide the official citation first, followed by the citation to the appendix.
Introduce the appendix reference with the phrase 'reprinted in'.
Indicate the statute revision or volume to which the appendix is attached, followed by a comma and the appendix number.
Write the appendix number in Roman numerals.
examples: Canadian Bill of Rights, SC 1960, c 44, reprinted in RSC 1985, Appendix III.

rules: When referring to Indigenous constitution documents, include critical information so that readers can track the source.
If the document title is not in English or French, provide a description in parentheses or a translation in square brackets.
Do not italicize such information.
examples: Sto:lo Xwexwilmexw Shxwelmexwelh [Sto:lo People's Constitution], (2020), online: <sxta.bc.ca> [perma.cc/X9BT-7PAA].
